items.body: Label: Shifting Paradigm Records, 2026 Personnel - Bryan Murray: tenor saxophone; Adam Linz: bass; Dan Monaghan: drums. Boasting a catchy sound and enjoying genuine freedom within the structure, saxophonist and composer Bryan Murray leads a supple chord-less jazz trio featuring bassist Adam Linz and longtime associate drummer Dan Monaghan. With friendship and collaboration at the center of Wolf , Murray—who also leads the peculiar avant-garde-meets-country band Bryan and the Haggards, is a member of Moppa Elliott’s Unspeakable Garbage, and has performed with David Byrne and St. Vincent outside the jazz sphere—explores his own music, radiating energy and abandon in a way that keeps listeners fully engaged. “ Bombs ” kicks off with hooky, motivic saxophone firepower over agile drums and sturdy bass, channeling David S. Ware and the reed language of Threadgill’s Air over the tight-knit rhythmic web spun by Linz and Monaghan. Post-bop and avant-garde walk hand in hand here, while “ Curtain ”, delivered with a sensitive balladic touch, brings forth Monaghan’s mallet work and shimmering cymbal washes. There’s pensive lyricism cutting through the open spaces, and Murray’s cautious melody is closely shadowed by Linz. Evoking childhood memories in West Virginia, “ Dirtslide ” displays an irreverent, hard-bop-inflected elegance over a full-throttle swing that is briefly suspended to accommodate the conversational interaction between Linz and Monaghan. Tactical bass mobility and crisp drumming dominate until Murray’s return, his playing abounding in ideas, supported by a firmly grounded and energetic rhythm section. The folksy theme of this piece contrasts with the pure modal jazz of “ Buell ”, a passionate prayer that recalls the spiritual hymns of John Coltrane and Billy Harper. “ Cloud Shapes ” is anchored by Linz’s impeccable bass guidance, while Monaghan’s cymbal work and mallets transport us to distant worlds. Murray’s narrative gift is unmistakable here. The title track, “ Wolf ”, achieves an air of mystery through a simple yet relentless bass ostinato. Deliberately measured, it unfolds in a lugubrious 3/4, while the closer, “ Fill Taker ”, embraces avant-garde elasticity, with Murray’s authoritative presence enhanced by well-delineated lines and motifs over a vibrant rhythmic foundation. This is stirring, serious sax-bass-drums work, resulting in a contemporary jazz album well worth digging into. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Bombs ► 03 - Dirtslide ► 05 - Buell ► 08 - Fill Taker

items.body:
LAUNCHPAD officially stepped into the spotlight on 3 August with its inaugural media event at PJ Performing Arts Centre in Kuala Lumpur, introducing a new artist growth platform designed to help emerging acts expand their reach across Southeast Asia.

Developed by Fast Track Entertainment in partnership with Sony Music Malaysia, LAUNCHPAD brings together intimate live showcases, regional media exposure, original digital content and brand partnerships to support artists as they grow beyond their home markets.

The official unveiling welcomed members of the media, industry partners and invited guests for the platform's first public introduction, while highlighting its vision of creating stronger connections between artists, audiences and the wider entertainment ecosystem across the region.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by GOKPOP (@gokpop_gallery)

The event featured appearances from KIIRAS, the six-member global K-pop girl group from South Korea; UPRIZE, Vietnam's rising seven-member boy group; and Malaysian entertainment icon Yusry Abdul Halim, who also participated in the programme alongside representatives from Fast Track Entertainment and Sony Music Malaysia. Live showcase performances and exclusive media interview sessions gave attendees an early look at the platform's artist-first approach.

Speaking during the launch, Fast Track Entertainment CEO Harris Lim shared that LAUNCHPAD represents an important milestone in the company's vision of building a more connected entertainment ecosystem across Southeast Asia. He said the platform was created around intimate live showcase experiences that connect artists directly with audiences, media, brands and industry partners, while creating new commercial opportunities that support long-term regional growth.

Unlike traditional artist development initiatives, LAUNCHPAD is designed to extend beyond the stage. Each showcase will be supported by regional media engagement, original digital content, industry networking and brand collaborations, helping artists strengthen their visibility and build sustainable careers across Southeast Asia.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by LAUNCHPAD (@launchpadexperience)

Following its official unveiling, LAUNCHPAD is set to roll out showcase editions across Southeast Asia from late 2026 through early 2027, with more participating artists, locations and programme details to be announced in the coming months.

AXEAN Festival 2026 will take over Jimbaran Hub in Bali, Indonesia, on 29–30 August, bringing together artists and music industry professionals from across Asia and beyond.

The lineup features D’MASIV, Ndarboy Genk, Arivu, Masdo, and Nerd Connection, alongside regional favourites Subsonic Eye, PLAYERTWO, Yellow Fang, Crystal Murray, ALYSON, and Basboi.

Spanning indie rock, alternative pop, hip-hop, soul, electronic jazz, progressive rock, dream pop, and contemporary Asian sounds, the bill will also include Aelea, Babon, Basajan, Bishnu Paneru, brkfstblend, Cactus Cactus, can't be Blue, Ciggarats, Clever Moose, Cupnoodle, Drizzly, El Karmoya, Emptyyy, Feral Stripes, GEE EXCLSV, GENIUS Flow, Given, hailinhtasm, INSPIRATIVE, Jo Soegono, Laze and Mardial, Lil Asian Thiccie x dj magn3sium, Littlefingers, Litty, LOR, Mayu, MRCH, Noni, Novocrane, Pitahati, Satu Per Empat, Scamper, Silly Silky, SLOWWVES, sub:shaman, Treaks, and YuuHai.

Gavendri and Olsam are also scheduled to deliver special performances at the festival’s invite-only opening party.

One of this edition’s biggest milestones is the Asian debut of Live on KEXP. The Seattle-based public radio station and music platform KEXP will record exclusive live sessions with selected artists during the festival.

The partnership aims to help independent artists from Southeast Asia reach wider international audiences by bringing KEXP’s recording team directly to the region.

AXEAN Festival will also host KOREA SPOTLIGHT, the K-music showcase presented by South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Creative Content Agency.

can't be Blue, MRCH, Nerd Connection, and Silly Silky will make their Indonesian debuts as part of the programme. All four artists emerged from MUSE ON, KOCCA’s artist discovery and development initiative, and will also appear at a dedicated KOREA SPOTLIGHT showcase in Jakarta.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AXEAN Festival (@axeanfestival)

This year will also see the introduction of SEA URBAN, a programme dedicated to Southeast Asia’s hip-hop, rap, R&B, and contemporary urban music scenes.

The programme will combine a curated artist showcase with an industry panel examining the region’s evolving identities, rapid growth, and increasing global reach.

Festivalgoers can also expect an expanded songwriting camp and a Southeast Asian hawker-inspired food experience, adding more opportunities for collaboration and cultural exchange beyond the performances.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AXEAN Festival (@axeanfestival)

Launched in 2020, AXEAN Festival has featured 200 artists from 20 countries across its first six editions. It has also welcomed 420 delegates from 32 countries and drawn close to 18,000 attendees to its in-person events.

For generations of Singaporeans, National Day songs have served as more than ceremonial singalongs. They've become part of the country's collective memory, tied to school assemblies, National Day Parade celebrations, and moments of shared pride. With Celebrating Singapore: Volume 3, Music & Drama Company (MDC) isn't looking to replace those memories—it is inviting listeners to hear them through a fresh lens.

Released as the third instalment in MDC's Celebrating Singapore series, the four-track tribute album takes familiar National Day Parade classics and reimagines them with contemporary pop production inspired by international artists such as Michael Jackson, Maroon 5, Zara Larsson, and Shila Amzah. The result is a collection that bridges nostalgia with modern musical sensibilities while introducing these songs to a younger audience.

Rather than opting for straightforward remakes, each track embraces a distinct sonic identity.

Opening the record, 'Reach Out For The Skies' swaps its stadium-ready energy for a groove rooted in the disco-funk spirit of Michael Jackson's Off The Wall. Performed by RINES alongside aküma, the reworked version retains the optimism of the original while adding a rhythm that feels equally suited to today's playlists.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

Elsewhere, aküma returns on 'Breathing City', where producer Weiwen Seah draws from the restrained emotional pull of Maroon 5's 'This Love'. The production strips things back with expressive piano and understated instrumentation, pushing the singer into unfamiliar territory and showcasing a different side of his genre-blending artistry.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

Dominic Chin steps into the spotlight with 'Shine On Me', a soaring reinterpretation inspired by the grandeur of Shila Amzah's celebrated 'Yang Cong' performance. The arrangement gradually builds towards a cinematic climax, transforming the National Day anthem into something that feels equally at home on a concert stage.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

Perhaps the album's biggest surprise arrives with Gail Belmonte's rendition of 'Home'. One of Singapore's most beloved songs is given an EDM makeover before erupting into a dubstep-infused chorus inspired by Zara Larsson's 'Midnight Sun'. It's an ambitious rework that demonstrates how even the country's most recognisable anthem can evolve without losing its emotional core.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Music & Drama Company (MDC) (@musicanddramacompany)

The project also highlights a cross-section of Singapore's contemporary music scene. Alongside established performers like Dominic Chin and Gail Belmonte, the album spotlights rising voices including aküma and RINES, whose individual musical identities bring new perspectives to songs many listeners already know by heart.

More than a nostalgia project, Celebrating Singapore: Volume 3 presents a conversation between generations. By pairing iconic National Day songs with modern production styles and homegrown talent, MDC demonstrates how familiar melodies can continue to resonate long after their original debut—reminding listeners that national anthems, much like music itself, can keep evolving with the people who sing them.

Celebrating Singapore: Volume 3 is available on all major listening platforms including Kakee, Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. For more information on MDC, visit its social media platforms Facebook, Instagram and TikTok.

items.body:
National Day Parade 2026 is set to transform the National Stadium into one enormous stage on 9 August, bringing together 36 artistes and more than 2,600 performers for Singapore’s 61st birthday.

Returning to the venue for the first time in a decade, this year’s show is framed around the theme Majulah Singapura, Go Beyond!. Across its pre-parade programme and six chapters, audiences can expect everything from electro-pop and Karnatik music to vintage Singapore tunes, beloved television themes and stadium-sized singalongs.

Hosting the evening are Joakim Gomez, Hafidz Rahman, Udaya Soundari, Xixi Lim and Gurmit Singh. William Xavier, affectionately known as Mr X, returns as the “Voice of NDP”. He will be joined by first-time NDP announcer Joanna François.

The celebration also arrives with the first Go Beyond: NDP 2026 Album, which brings together original compositions and reimagined favourites. Spanning uplifting anthems, heartfelt ballads, contemporary pop and electronic music, its songs form part of the show’s journey through Singapore’s heritage, shared memories and hopes for the future.

Pre-Parade

Before the parade officially begins, the hosts will welcome audiences back to the National Stadium with a series of singalongs and warm-up activities.

The programme includes a rehearsal of ‘Giants’, written by weish and performed by Iman Fandi, followed by the ‘Singapore Town–Tapau’ medley. Audiences can also expect quizzes, an introduction to this year’s NDP Pack and a segment marking the 60th anniversary of the National Pledge.

As NDP goes live, the cinematic Flag Relay film will follow the National Flag through Singapore’s heartlands and familiar locations. The action will then move from screen to stadium as the flag enters the venue for a live relay.

Athletes and para-athletes from Team Singapore will carry the flag around the stage alongside student-athletes from the Singapore Sports School. The relay will feature prominent sporting figures including Paralympic swimmer Yip Pin Xiu, kitefoiler Max Maeder and indoor skydiver Kai Minejima-Lee.

Chapter One: Go Beyond Self

The Go Beyond Self chapter places the spotlight on the Parade and Ceremony, which will feature 32 contingents and the largest civilian parade participation in more than a decade.

The proceedings will begin with the entry of the Guard of Honour, Colours Party and Combined Band. The Guard of Honour comprises contingents from the Army, Navy, Air Force, Digital and Intelligence Service, Singapore Police Force and Singapore Civil Defence Force.

The Combined Band brings together musicians from the Singapore Armed Forces Central Band, Singapore Police Force Band, Singapore National Cadet Corps Command Band and National Police Cadet Corps Band.

Collectively, the parade’s contingents will represent all six pillars of Total Defence, reflecting the role that Singaporeans play in keeping the country strong.

Key ceremonial moments include the State Flag Flypast, Feu De Joie and the 21-Gun Presidential Gun Salute. For the first time, the salute will be fired afloat at Kallang Basin.

Chapter Two: Go Beyond the Ordinary

The Go Beyond the Ordinary chapter begins with the SAF Band carrying the show out of the ceremonial proceedings through a stirring musical transition. Its performance will be accompanied by a high-energy routine from Martial House.

At the centre of the chapter is the People’s Parade, a colourful procession celebrating everyday Singaporeans whose service, passion and dedication have made a difference to those around them.

Eighteen floats will move through the performance space, representing six foundational values: Protect, Provide, Create, Build, Care and Justice.

Following a humorous skit involving the hosts, the chapter will conclude with a musical face-off between Ric Liu and the Shiok Sistas. The two sides will trade local tunes in a friendly competition, with spectators invited to join in using their voices and thundersticks.

Also appearing in the chapter are Jackie Pereira, Jalyn Han, Alin Mosbit and Annetha Ayyavoo.

The production will feature performers from Unity Secondary School, Beatty Secondary , Edgefield Secondary School, Tampines Meridian Junior College and St Andrew’s Junior College.

Chapter Three: Go Beyond Our Size

The Go Beyond Our Size chapter shifts from the high-energy mood of the People’s Parade into a more reflective exploration of Singapore’s maritime heritage, cultural roots and connections with the world.

It begins with a cinematic film about the nation’s relationship with the sea, followed by Asnida Daud performing ‘Aok Diko’, meaning “Yes, Of Course”. Sung in the Orang Laut dialect, the piece explores coastal identity, belonging and Singapore’s connection to its waters.

Asnida will be accompanied by a multi-ethnic group of drummers and 700 performers from Soka Gakkai Singapore. Larger-than-life puppets depicting native animals, including the tapir and mousedeer, will bring local folklore and biodiversity into the stadium.

Sushma Soma will follow with a Karnatik ode to Singapore. Marine-animal puppets and trading ships will move through the performance space, transforming the stadium floor into an underwater and seafaring spectacle.

Electronic duo NADA will then bring Singapore’s musical past into conversation with the present, fusing nostalgic local sounds with contemporary electronic beats. The act will be represented by Safuan Johari.

For the chapter’s finale, Asnida, Sushma and NADA will unite for ‘Song for Singapore’. The multi-ethnic drummers will return to join the artistes and Soka Gakkai performers for the musical conclusion.

Rizman Putra is also part of the chapter’s artiste lineup. Its performing partners include Damaru Singapore, the Eurasian Drum Ensemble, Nadi Singapura and ZingO Festival Drum Group.

Chapter Four: Go Beyond Time

The Go Beyond Time chapter turns the National Stadium into a television time machine, revisiting the programmes, songs, personalities and campaigns that have shaped Singapore’s popular culture.

The chapter begins with a short film depicting the five hosts as children in a 1960s kampong, encountering television for the first time.

Joakim Gomez will then perform an excerpt from ‘A World of Tomorrows’, followed by Hafidz Rahman dancing to the opening theme from Mat Yoyo.

Gurmit Singh will step back into the unmistakable yellow boots of Phua Chu Kang, while Xixi Lim will perform ‘Moonlight in the City’, or ‘城里的月光’. Udaya Soundari will close the main sequence with the theme from the Vasantham police drama Vettai.

Najip Ali will add another blast from the past with ‘Ren-tak Oonik’.

More than 300 performers from the People’s Association will bring the chapter to life alongside the Music and Drama Company, Singapore Airlines staff and mascots inspired by memorable national campaigns.

Together, the performances form a playful channel-surf through the television memories and cultural touchpoints that have connected generations of Singaporeans.

Chapter Five: Go Beyond Our Limits

The Go Beyond Our Limits chapter launches NDP into the future with electronic music, aerial choreography and the parade’s first indoor drone light show.

It opens with a kinetic typography film featuring words associated with Singapore’s culture. The chapter then shifts into high gear as Jasmine Sokko descends onto the stage alongside two aerialists while performing ‘You’ll Be Okay’.

Three hundred drones will move in synchrony with the performers 30 metres above the ground, combining music, technology and movement in one of the evening’s biggest visual spectacles.

The electronic momentum will continue with Han Oh and ‘Zero G-Roll’. Seven dancers will rise through stage lifts for a tightly synchronised routine matching the track’s electronic pulse.

Ranging from eight to 29 years old, the group includes an autistic dancer and a dancer with Down syndrome. The performers also represent Singapore’s four major ethnic groups.

Singer-songwriter Sky Shen will bring the chapter to a close with ‘March On With Me’, accompanied by six vocalists from the Music and Drama Company and dancers from Ministry of Education schools.

The performance will provide a reflective transition into the final chapter of the show.

Chapter Six: Go Beyond, Together

The concluding Go Beyond, Together chapter brings the evening’s music, sporting spirit and message of collective progress together.

It begins with Roar!, a short documentary centred on the stories of four sports coaches and the perseverance of Singapore’s sporting community.

The film will lead into Iman Fandi’s performance of ‘Giants’ alongside the 61-member The People’s Choir. Sixty-one coaches and athletes will also take the stage, connecting the song’s message of lifting one another up with the determination of Singapore’s sporting community.

The mood will then shift from reflective to celebratory as Gareth Fernandez, Dru Chen and The People’s Choir perform ‘Sparkle’, an upbeat singalong centred on individuality, confidence and togetherness.

Irene Jansen will also appear as part of the finale chapter’s artiste lineup.

The show will then move into the Majulah Moment, when Singaporeans will be invited to recite the National Pledge and sing the National Anthem.

Finally, DJ LENERD will lead a stadium-wide singalong featuring rearranged National Day songs, bringing the evening to an exuberant close.

Across its six chapters, NDP 2026 presents Singapore not through one definitive musical style, but through a chorus of traditions, generations and communities.

From Asnida Daud’s exploration of Orang Laut identity and Sushma Soma’s Karnatik performance to Jasmine Sokko’s aerial electro-pop spectacle and Iman Fandi’s stadium-sized rendition of ‘Giants’, this year’s show is shaping up to be both a celebration of how far Singapore has come and an invitation to imagine where it might go next.

kiOra took their first step onto the international stage with an opening performance at CENTRAL MUSIC & ENTERTAINMENT FESTIVAL in Kuala Lumpur on 1 August.

Performing at Zepp Kuala Lumpur, the four-member Japanese girl group appeared before a Malaysian audience for their first-ever show outside Japan. The set marked a major milestone for kiOra as they introduced their music and self-described “Tokyo Hyper City Pop” sound to fans overseas.

The group performed their debut single, 'Coco', with the crowd’s cheers leaving a strong impression on the members.

“Getting to perform kiOra’s first song 'Coco' and sing it together with everyone was amazing! Jom jumpa lagi!” OTO shared after the show.

KYLA added, “Thank you to everyone who came today! It was the best. The 'Coco' MV is coming out soon, so please get ready to watch and rewatch! Can’t wait to meet again.”

RUKA also reflected on the audience’s response, saying, “I was so happy to hear your cheers during our first overseas performance. I hope we can sing 'Coco' together again!”

YU shared, “I was energized by today’s CENTRAL performance. I’ll keep doing my best to share our first single 'Coco' with even more people around the world!”

The Kuala Lumpur appearance followed kiOra’s unveiling at HEAD IN THE CLOUDS Tokyo, where the group first introduced its blend of hyperpop and city pop influences.

During their CENTRAL appearance, kiOra also announced that the official music video for 'Coco' will premiere worldwide on 8 August, alongside the single’s digital release.

'Coco' draws its title from the phrase “in my core” and the Japanese words “ima coco”, meaning “here and now”. The track centres on embracing one’s present self and finding the courage to move forward before feeling fully ready.

The single was created with producers and songwriters her0ism, Yaeji, Mechatok and Kanata Okajima, with Chelsea Warner joining the songwriting team. Recording took place at StudioBeat3, while vocal production was handled by Ashley Alish.

Massive Attack have issued a statement following their Singapore concert on 29 July, claiming that the entire touring party was detained and questioned by police after the show.

In the statement, the British trip-hop group said its members were isolated and questioned separately following their performance at The Star Theatre. The band also alleged that some members had their hotel rooms searched and passports temporarily confiscated.

The account adds new details to the controversy, which began after Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall displayed a Palestinian flag near the end of the concert.

Massive Attack also addressed reports that the band had led the audience in chanting “Free Palestine”.

According to the group, large sections of the audience spontaneously began the chant before the band took the stage and again at the end of the show. The statement described the crowd’s response as an “organic” expression of solidarity rather than one directed by the performers.

The band said it had not expected holding up the Palestinian flag to breach local laws, describing Palestine as “a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries”.

The Singapore Police Force and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) previously announced that two unnamed members had been issued stern warnings for offences under the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act and the Public Order Act.

The two musicians were also barred from re-entering Singapore. In view of the entry ban, IMDA said it would not approve future applications for Massive Attack to perform in the country.

IMDA is separately investigating possible breaches of the concert’s licence conditions, including a condition prohibiting the display of flags in support of causes.

In their response, Massive Attack said they were “proud” to have shared the moment with their Singaporean audience, whom they praised for showing solidarity with Palestinians despite the potential consequences.

The group also criticised the wider international response to the war in Gaza and described the experience in Singapore as a reminder of the need to defend human rights and freedom of expression.

Massive Attack called on the Singapore government to ratify the United Nations International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and allow citizens to express their conscience “without fear of state prosecution”.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Massive Attack (@massiveattackofficial)

Despite their criticism of the authorities’ actions, the band thanked concertgoers for making them feel welcome during their visit.

They closed the statement with: “As we were saying … Free Palestine.”

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.

For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
